title: White House Signals No Letup in Hardline Immigration Enforcement Despite Midterm Reversal
snippet: Despite devastating midterm election losses and a voter backlash over aggressive deportation tactics, the Trump administration is doubling down on its hardline immigration agenda under the leadership of White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller.
content:
WASHINGTON — Despite a sharp rebuke at the ballot box during the recent midterm elections, the Trump administration has no plans to ease up on its sweeping immigration crackdown, according to multiple U.S. officials familiar with internal deliberations.

With immigration hawk Stephen Miller elevated to White House chief of staff, administration insiders say federal agencies are proceeding full speed ahead with ambitious arrest and deportation targets. If anything, officials suggest the White House may lean further into its signature policy rather than retreat.

Voter Backlash Meets Executive Resolve

The decision to maintain the current trajectory comes in the wake of significant Republican losses across the country, including defeat in key political battlegrounds like Texas. Exit polling revealed widespread voter discontent with federal enforcement tactics, with 58% of voters nationwide stating the administration's deportation blitz had gone too far. Texas Latinos, concerned with both economic issues and aggressive enforcement, swung heavily toward Democratic candidates.

When asked whether the election results would trigger a strategy shift, one official familiar with White House operations offered a blunt assessment: "I would count on the opposite with Miller as chief of staff."

Administration officials reportedly view the midterm losses through a different lens, attributing the defeat primarily to voter anxieties over inflation, the broader economy, and foreign conflict rather than public pushback against immigration raids.

White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis reinforced the administration's stance, emphasizing that the president remains committed to border enforcement and removing unauthorized immigrants. Department of Homeland Security officials echoed that sentiment, confirming that Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has received no orders to scale back operations.

High Targets and Broad Powers

Operational targets reflect that commitment. Directives issued to ICE field offices prior to the election set aggressive goals of approximately 19,000 arrests per week—or roughly 2,700 per day—up significantly from earlier benchmarks.

The central driver behind the relentless push is Miller, the chief architect of President Trump's immigration portfolio for nearly a decade. Since taking over as chief of staff, Miller has expanded his influence across executive policymaking, overseeing measures that have functionally dismantled the U.S. asylum framework, curtailed refugee admissions, and intensified visible community-level arrests.

Those enforcement operations have not been without controversy. High-profile raids have sparked intense public outrage, particularly following an incident in Minneapolis earlier this year that resulted in the deaths of two American citizens, prompting temporary adjustments after bipartisan protests.

Headwinds Await in a Divided Washington

The administration's unwavering stance sets up a major clash come January, when Democrats assume control of both chambers of Congress. Lawmakers are expected to launch aggressive oversight investigations, issue subpoenas targeting DHS officials, and attempt to attach spending restrictions to future budget bills.

At the local level, newly elected leaders are already taking steps to distance their municipalities from federal enforcement efforts. In Houston, local leadership announced plans to curtail police collaboration with federal immigration authorities following the election outcome.

However, policy analysts note that congressional Democrats face steep structural hurdles in trying to rein in the agency. President Trump retains veto power over legislative funding restrictions, and ICE remains fortified by a massive $75 billion multi-year funding package passed during the previous legislative session.

"They're going to continue apace," said Theresa Cardinal Brown, a former DHS official now focusing on immigration policy. "They have the money. They have the resources."
